title: Loft 4 — racing pigeons: young birds with cheesy throat lesions
presentation: A racing loft of sixty birds. Eight youngsters are losing weight, standing fluffed with wet beaks, and one has a yellow cheesy mass visible at the back of the throat. Two squabs have died in the nest.

stages.title: Examine the birds and the loft
stages.briefing: Affected youngsters: BCS 2/5, wet beaks with ropy saliva, reluctant to swallow, one with a yellow caseous plaque at the oropharynx and another with a swelling under the mandible. Crops slow to empty. Two nestling deaths. Loft: communal water trough refilled every other day, adults feeding young by crop milk, birds recently returned from a race and mixed with residents.
stages.prompt: Which findings point to trichomoniasis rather than a respiratory disease?

options.label: Yellow caseous oropharyngeal plaques
options.detail: The classic canker lesion

options.label: Ropy saliva with reluctance to swallow
options.detail: Oesophageal and crop involvement

options.label: Nestlings dying while being fed crop milk by adults
options.detail: Vertical transmission from carrier parents

options.label: Communal water trough refilled every other day
options.detail: The transmission route — history, not a clinical sign

options.label: Fluffed posture and weight loss
options.detail: Non-specific illness in any pigeon

stages.explanation: Caseous plaques in the throat with ropy saliva is canker, and the nestling deaths are the same disease arriving by crop milk from apparently healthy adults. That last point is what makes it a loft problem: the adults look well and are the reservoir. The shared water is the other route and it is the easiest thing on the list to fix.

stages.title: Choose the tests
stages.briefing: You are at the loft with a microscope, warm saline and slides.

options.label: Warm saline wet mount from a crop or oropharyngeal swab, examined immediately
options.detail: Motile trophozoites, seen live

options.label: Sample several birds including apparently healthy adults
options.detail: Finds the carriers driving the outbreak

options.label: Crop swab cytology stained for yeasts and bacteria
options.detail: Candida and Gram-negative co-infection

options.label: Faecal examination for coccidia and worms
options.detail: The usual concurrent burdens in a loft

options.label: Post-mortem of the dead squabs including liver
options.detail: Systemic spread shows in the liver

options.label: Paramyxovirus serology as the primary test
options.detail: A vaccination question for the loft, not the cause of throat plaques

options.label: Blood culture from affected youngsters
options.detail: Not how this diagnosis is made, and impractical at the loft

stages.explanation: This diagnosis is made in ninety seconds with warm saline and a microscope, and it fails if the slide cools or if you wait — the trophozoites stop moving and become invisible. Swabbing healthy adults is what turns the diagnosis into a control plan, and looking for concurrent coccidia and worms reflects how these lofts actually present.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Warm saline wet mounts: numerous motile, pear-shaped flagellated protozoa in six of eight sick youngsters and in four of ten clinically-healthy adults. Cytology: mixed bacteria, no significant yeast. Faecal: light coccidial oocyst load, no strongyle eggs. Post-mortem of squabs: caseous oesophageal plaques with pale hepatic foci. Water trough biofilm heavy on inspection.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: Trichomonas gallinae infection in the loft
options.detail: Motile trophozoites in sick birds

options.label: Healthy adults are carriers and the source for the squabs
options.detail: Positive wet mounts in birds with no signs

options.label: Systemic spread in the squabs that died
options.detail: Hepatic foci with oesophageal plaques

options.label: The communal water trough is maintaining transmission
options.detail: Heavy biofilm in a trough refilled every other day

options.label: Coccidiosis is the primary problem
options.detail: A light oocyst load does not explain caseous throat plaques

options.label: Candidiasis is the primary problem
options.detail: No significant yeast on cytology

stages.explanation: Positive slides from birds with no clinical signs is the finding that shapes everything: treat only the sick youngsters and the carriers will re-infect them and the next round of squabs. The hepatic lesions in the squabs show why nestlings die rather than merely fail to thrive, and the biofilm explains why the loft cannot clear it between races.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: Motile trophozoites in sick youngsters and in symptom-free adults, caseous oesophageal plaques with hepatic foci in dead squabs, light coccidial load, no yeast, heavy trough biofilm.

options.label: Trichomoniasis (canker) with carrier adults maintaining loft infection
options.detail: The organism, the reservoir and the route

options.label: Candidiasis of the crop
options.detail: No significant yeast on cytology

options.label: Coccidiosis
options.detail: A light load, and the wrong lesions

options.label: Wet pox (avian pox, diphtheritic form)
options.detail: Produces similar plaques, but motile protozoa identify the cause here

options.label: Bacterial ingluvitis
options.detail: Mixed bacteria are secondary to the protozoal lesions

stages.explanation: Because the carriers are the problem, the treatment is loft-wide — carnidazole or ronidazole for every bird, not just the eight that look ill — with the trough cleaned and refilled daily, and treatment timed before breeding and after races. A diagnosis that stops at "canker in eight youngsters" produces a relapse within a month.
